detail.title: Reliability-Centered Evaluation of Sparse Longitudinal CT Lesion-Size Forecasting with Conformal Interval Calibration and Gompertz-Inspired Regularization
detail.abstract: Sparse longitudinal CT follow-up makes lesion-size forecasting difficult when only a few prior observations are available, and prediction error alone does not fully capture forecast reliability. We investigated the value of additional longitudinal history under a fixed prediction horizon and examined whether predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency improve together. Methods: We constructed a five-visit same-lesion benchmark from DeepLesion and Deep Lesion Tracker, comprising 205 trajectories from 129 patients after patient- and scan-level quality control. The primary analysis fixed the most recent observation at T_3 and predicted the common T_3-to-T_4 log-size change while progressively adding earlier observations. We compared deterministic prediction, a cohort-level Gaussian process, MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and a Gaussian residual-scale baseline, and further evaluated patient-level conformal calibration and Gompertz-inspired trajectory regularization. Results: Under the fixed-horizon design, mean held-out RMSE across ten training seeds was 0.4726, 0.4305, 0.4499, and 0.4513 for m=1,2,3,4, respectively, with no further improvement beyond m=2. Methods with similar point-prediction accuracy showed different uncertainty behavior. At m=4, raw coverage from the cohort-level feature GP was close to the 95% nominal level, whereas MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and residual-scale intervals were conservative. Patient-level conformal calibration generally achieved near-nominal or conservative coverage, but with wider intervals. Development cross-validation selected no Gompertz-inspired regularization, and the population reference often disagreed with lesion-level change directions; the nonzero regularized comparison also showed no consistent improvement in accuracy or uncertainty reliability on the held-out test set. Conclusions: Once the visit-index prediction horizon was controlled, more remote history provided limited additional predictive value. Predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and agreement with a trajectory prior captured distinct aspects of model performance and should be evaluated separately in sparse longitudinal imaging.

title: Birth, Life, and Death of AI Models
affiliations: ,  and MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL)

detail.title: Birth, Life, and Death of AI Models
detail.abstract: We characterize the lifecycles of open-weight AI models using a weekly panel of the 108,074 most-downloaded models on Hugging Face, which together account for 99.5 percent of the platform's more than 53 billion downloads. We link these data to token usage from OpenRouter and performance rankings from Arena and Artificial Analysis. We establish key institutional details about the supply of and demand for AI models, and we organize our analysis into three phases: birth, life, and death. In the "birth" phase, we show that major developers often release models in batches, concurrently introducing models that are both vertically differentiated (e.g., by size, capability, and latency) and horizontally differentiated (e.g., by task specialization, hardware compatibility, and alignment). Because weights are open, developers can also build on one another's models. We document cumulative innovation through fine-tuned, quantized, merged and adapted descendants of source models. In the "life" phase, we quantify how demand evolves after release. Even within the sample of top models, demand is concentrated, and the concentration persists: the median model loses ∼68 percent of its release-week downloads within ten weeks, while the most popular models decline gradually; as a result, the top percentile's advantage over the median model is ∼600-fold at release, and ∼900-fold six months later. Further, we estimate spillover effects from new popular model releases on related models and find that the first popular third-party descendant is associated with a 76 to 99 percent increase in weekly downloads of its source model. In the "death" phase, we construct measures of technical obsolescence and usage obsolescence. We find that technical obsolescence is associated with a slow but persistent decrease in demand, while usage obsolescence coincides with an immediate but temporary drop in demand. Our findings characterize open-weight AI as a market of complementary model portfolios, one in which third-party developers building on a source model can raise demand for the original, and in which demand is slow to respond to technical obsolescence.

detail.abstract: Community engagement in residential elder care is often organized as donations, festival events, or isolated visits. Such activity can meet immediate needs, but its visibility does not show whether residents experience choice, recognition, continuity, or connection. This structured integrative evidence synthesis examines Indian and international scholarship published primarily from 2016 to September 2026, while retaining two foundational earlier sources, on residential elder care, dignity, social connection, volunteering, intergenerational engagement, and frontline relationships. Targeted searches of PubMed, PubMed Central, publisher and DOI-linked pages, institutional reports, and reference lists were synthesized across need, support, mediation, outcomes, and implementation. Three recurring findings emerged: material security does not assure relational well-being; activity benefits depend on continuity, resident choice, and fit; and sustained engagement requires coordination, role clarity, feedback, and inclusion. The article uses these findings to identify five linked translation processes: need recognition, respectful entry, repeated presence, practical mediation, and institutional learning. Through these processes, episodic assistance may become relational infrastructure. The resulting analytical model shifts evaluation from the visibility of giving to the quality and durability of connection. It offers testable propositions and an implementation-focused research agenda for residential elder care in India.

detail.abstract:
We consider the convergence of the quadratic form in independent, not necessarily identically distributed, centred random variables weighted by a real symmetric matrix V with a non-vanishing diagonal. Its central limit theorem requires a Lindeberg-type condition on the eigenvalues of V. 
While previous studies relied on intricate, element-wise conditions on the weighting matrix V to obtain non-Gaussian limit laws, we prove an asymptotic invariance principle under a single joint eigenvalue-eigenvector condition. 
Assuming uniformly bounded fourth moments, we show that the quadratic form is asymptotically equivalent to the corresponding Gaussian quadratic form. Depending on the normalised asymptotic spectral tail variance of V, the quadratic form converges to a Gaussian, a generalised chi-squared distribution, or a weighted convolution of these two. 
We establish the universality of these results using a Lindeberg replacement approach with characteristic functions, complemented by an alternative method-of-moments proof, under stronger assumptions.

title:
The Chains We Choose

detail.title:
The Chains We Choose

detail.abstract: This is the fourth paper in a series that opened with An Ideal Society, which named four pillars a fair and prosperous society requires and left the fourth "a civilizationally-grounded liberty" the thinnest of them, asserted rather than built. This paper builds it. It takes Rousseau's observation that man is born free and everywhere in chains, and takes seriously his own resolution: that a chain is legitimate only when it is self-authored by those it binds. Liberty, on this reading, is not the absence of constraint but a test of whose constraint it is. The paper then confronts the danger built into that resolution, that self-authorship is the exact language every tyranny uses to describe the chains it imposes, and answers it by insisting that self-authorship be verifiable, through the same four-part accountability architecture the earlier papers in the series relied on. It argues that self-authorship, the dignity floor, and the accountability mechanisms are not separate tests run one after another but a single system in which removing any part breaks the rest. It grounds the claim in real cases: South Korea's citizens authoring their own political order at mortal cost in 1987; Switzerland, Taiwan, and Estonia deepening self-authorship with available technology; and Switzerland's own 2009 minaret referendum as the honest hard case, where a genuine majority authored a chain that still crossed the floor for a minority the process never actually reached. It shows the same tension, legitimate self-rule bounded by something no consent may cross, worked out independently across Persian, Chinese, Korean, Japanese, Islamic, Indian, African, and Indigenous traditions, which is the paper's evidence for its central claim and not a decoration upon it. Throughout, an invented figure, an orchardist who loses a fair vote and consents to the chain anyway, carries the question the argument is finally about: not what the winner feels, but what the loser does. The paper closes, as the others have, by weighing honest benefits against risks left open, and with a call to those who build the institutions inside which people either recognize their own hand in what binds them, or do not.

detail.abstract: To address shortcomings of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation's (SFDR) de facto classification under Articles 8 and 9, the European Commission has proposed three voluntary product categories: Sustainable, Transition, and ESG Basics. Using a discrete choice experiment embedded in an online survey of broadly representative samples of experienced retail investors in France (n = 1,496) and Germany (n = 1,692), we examine whether investors consider these categories in their investment decisions and perceive them as reducing information frictions, increasing trust in sustainability-related product claims, and reducing greenwashing risks. The proposed categories are perceived as reducing information frictions, while gains in trust and reductions in perceived greenwashing risk are limited. detail.abstract: Antitrust enforcement has long been considered one of the most legally and economically complex areas of Supreme Court jurisprudence. The Supreme Court's landmark antitrust decisions through the 20 th Century developed the rules by which firms, here and abroad, knew they could compete within. However, in the 21 st Century, the European Union has overtaken the United States as the most up to date antitrust enforcement given new technological advancements. In the area of tying antitrust enforcement, the European Union has levied fines in the way of billions of dollars against Google for the action of forcing software bundles on other firms and consumers. This antitrust violation was recognized by the United States Department of Justice in a complaint against Google for the same bundling activities under an exclusive dealing claim, but no further action occurred after the complaint. This note finds that the Justice Department's classification of Google's activity as something other than a tying violation, combined with the Supreme Court's tying precedent being stuck in the 20 th Century, has signaled to big tech firms in America a new way to skirt antitrust enforcement while acting within outdated United States precedent.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to interrogate the doctrinal foundations of abuse of economic dependence, a liability standard newly introduced by Article 11 of the AfCFTA Protocol on Competition Policy, and to test its application to dominant digital platforms operating across African markets. It argues that dependence-based liability marks a genuine rupture from the dominance-centred paradigm inherited from Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, because it permits sanction without any finding of market power, resting instead on the relational weakness of a dependent counterparty. Drawing on the AfCFTA Protocol, the parallel COMESA Competition Regulations, and African-authored scholarship, the paper traces the doctrine's civil-law genealogy, its uneasy transplantation into a common-law-influenced continental architecture, and the interpretive ambiguities surrounding relative strength and significant effect. It critiques prevailing commentary for treating the doctrine as a simple gatekeeper add-on, and instead situates it within Africa's broader struggle against thin, concentrated digital markets. The paper concludes by proposing a structured evidentiary framework for African competition authorities confronting dependence claims involving ride-hailing, mobile money and social platforms.

detail.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has introduced significant changes to university writing practices and has challenged conventional approaches to writing instruction and academic support. Among the technologies attracting considerable attention is ChatGPT, which can generate, revise, summarize, explain, and reorganize written material within seconds. Its growing use by university students has created both opportunities and difficulties for writing centers, traditionally established to provide individualized assistance with writing development, critical thinking, revision, and communication skills. Rather than treating generative AI exclusively as a threat to academic writing, university writing centers can incorporate it into their services through carefully designed human-AI collaboration. This article examines how writing centers can transform their practices in response to ChatGPT while maintaining their educational mission. The discussion focuses on AI-assisted tutoring, writing development, academic integrity, critical thinking, tutor preparation, student agency, privacy, and responsible technology use. A conceptual methodology is employed, drawing on existing scholarship concerning writing center pedagogy, artificial intelligence in education, automated writing technologies, and academic integrity. The analysis suggests that writing centers can move beyond a conventional model based entirely on tutor-tostudent interaction toward a hybrid model in which human tutors guide students in evaluating, questioning, revising, and responsibly using AI-generated content. Such transformation requires clear institutional policies, AI literacy development, tutor training, transparent disclosure practices, and continued emphasis on the student's ownership of the writing process. The article argues that the educational value of writing centers does not disappear in an environment where AI can produce text; instead, their role can expand toward helping students become critical, ethical, and reflective participants in an increasingly AI-mediated academic environment.

detail.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a standard technique for grounding large language models (LLMs) in external, updatable knowledge, and the research literature around it has grown rapidly since the method was first introduced. Existing broad surveys, most notably Sharma [2025], provide a comprehensive taxonomy of RAG architectures spanning retriever design, generator design, hybrid approaches, and robustness techniques. However, the pace of publication in this area means that any snapshot survey is quickly followed by new work, and one specific sub-area-chunking and retrieval strategy selection-has seen a particularly dense cluster of empirical studies in late 2025 and 2026 that are not yet consolidated into a single reference. This paper serves two purposes. First, it briefly recaps the existing taxonomy of RAG architectures to orient readers new to the field. Second, and primarily, it synthesizes recent literature specifically on document chunking strategies, dense versus hybrid retrieval, and adaptive or self-correcting retrieval mechanisms, an area where recent empirical findings are notably inconsistent with one another. We present this literature in a structured comparative format, highlight where findings agree and disagree, and discuss the open challenges this disagreement implies for practitioners building RAG systems today. This paper is intended as a synthesis and reference document for practitioners and newcomers to the field rather than a report of novel experimental results.

detail.abstract: Municipal waste policy across the EU increasingly relies on making waste separation more convenient and on charging households for the waste they generate, yet comparable evidence from newer EU member states remains scarce. This study quantifies how two such measures, door-to-door (DtD) collection of recyclable fractions and Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) charging schemes that build on it, affect mixed municipal waste generation, separation effectiveness (the share of recyclables in total municipal waste), and the operational cost of waste management in the South Moravian Region, Czech Republic. Using cross-sectional data, the findings show that both PAYT charging schemes and door-to-door collection of recyclable fractions are associated with significantly lower mixed municipal waste per capita and higher separation effectiveness, with PAYT showing the strongest effect. In the estimates, DtD is associated with roughly 19 kg less mixed municipal waste per capita and PAYT with about 57 kg less. Both measures also raise operational waste-management costs, with one exception: the bag-based PAYT system combines the largest reduction in mixed waste and the greatest improvement in separation effectiveness with no significant cost increase, making it the most cost-effective option. Because PAYT in practice builds on DtD rather than replacing it, the two act as complements rather than alternatives. These mechanisms are especially relevant for transitioning countries and regions where waste separation is not yet firmly established.

detail.abstract: Do financial distress and credit access mediate the transmission of monetary policy to household expectations? I examine this question using data from the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations and its Credit Access Module, combining an event-study design around Federal Open Market Committee meetings with high-frequency monetary policy surprises from Jarociński and Karadi (2020). I find that credit access and financial health shape monetary policy transmission through distinct channels. Credit access shapes attention: households with credit access revise their interest rate expectations following monetary policy surprises, while households without it show no systematic response. Financial health governs interpretation: among households with credit access, only financially healthy households translate updated interest rate expectations into downward revisions of their inflation outlook, a reading consistent with the disinflationary intent of monetary tightening. Financially distressed households, despite holding credit cards, do not revise their inflation expectations coherently; instead, their revisions are markedly more dispersed, consistent with households reacting individually rather than converging on a common revision. These patterns are concentrated in the post-2020 inflationary episode; prior to 2020, monetary policy surprises generated little detectable updating for any group. Together, the results suggest that monetary policy transmits most effectively to financially healthy households, while financially distressed households attend to policy but interpret it less coherently.

detail.abstract: We ask how quickly the ability to predict a volatility regime decays when the forecaster's information is δ days out of date. On nine years of daily S&P 500 data, we evaluate four forecasters against a binary target, namely whether realised variance five days hence exceeds its trailing 252-day median, at delays of zero to 55 trading days. A trivial rule, "is volatility above its median now", stays above a constant forecast out to three days of delay against the more demanding of the two constants a forecaster could actually have run, and a week and a half against the weaker one, with the crossing itself unresolved at the next delay in each case; beyond that the data cannot separate it from a constant. Neither the Yang-Zhang estimator (+2.0 points at zero delay, 95% CI [-5.0, +8.2]) nor a walk-forward HAR classifier (-4.0 points, [-11.5, +2.5]) is distinguishable from it at any delay; the intervals are wide enough to leave a HAR advantage of up to 12.5 accuracy points unexcluded, so what is shown is a failure to separate and not an equality. We explain that instead of reporting it: for a median-split target, under approximate joint lognormality, the threshold rule is the Bayes rule among functions of the delayed state alone. Measured accuracies sit at 85-106% of that restricted-information Gaussian benchmark, exceeding it at six of ten delays, so Section 5 treats it as an approximation, never a ceiling. The benchmark is the best cut on the delayed state rather than the same-sign rule: the correlation turns negative at the two longest delays, where a same-sign rule is beaten by its own negation and is therefore not a benchmark for anything. The estimated headroom is small relative to sampling uncertainty in this sample, so the negative result is about the target, not the models. Three robustness checks follow, on the loss, the windows and the split. detail.abstract: The paper considers the problem of determining the relationship between the accounting system and economic cycles. Currently, the endogenous nature of accounting information is not discussed in papers on economic theory. The Bertomeu-Magee model is unique in that the regulation of accounting information quality acts as a factor explaining macroeconomic indicators such as the interest rate and the volume of lending in the economy. The designated model is based on a hypothesis that is not disclosed and strictly justified in the original article. Therefore, this study attempts to reveal the endogeneity of accounting information in the context of the history of its relationship with economic crises. It has been established that many accounting methods that initially distorted economic reality and led to inefficient capital allocation developed and became generally accepted in response to economic crises, which time after time exposed these contradictions to society. A hypothesis is formulated according to which a crisis (of a fundamental nature) in the financial sector of the economy is necessary for the next qualitative development of accounting. Using examples of "accounting errors", it is shown that current accounting practice does not allow determining the real profitability or loss-making of companies, while remaining institutionally legitimate. Despite the fact that economic agents are guided by the financial position of companies, perceptions of the latter are constructed in the form of accounting information, the philosophical and methodological foundations of which have been in a deep crisis for the last 60 years and are isolated from the modern discourse of economic science.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a quantitative, multi-vantage diagnostic of insecurity, conflict attribution, radicalisation, and terrorism perceptions in Mali. Drawing on parallel population (N = 1,876) and authority (N = 751) surveys, it treats insecurity and violence not as objective conditions to be causally explained, but as socially interpreted and morally evaluated phenomena. The analysis constructs graduated indices capturing perceived insecurity, conflict attribution repertoires, radicalisation salience, dialogue orientation, and terrorism framing, calculated separately for populations and authorities. Findings show that insecurity is widely experienced as a graded and relational condition rather than a binary state; conflict is primarily attributed to banditry and governance-related resource disputes rather than to identity or ideology; perceived increases in radicalisation are low among respondents willing to discuss the issue; and terrorism is framed predominantly through economic vulnerability and recruitment dynamics, with consistently low sympathy but non-trivial openness to dialogue. Convergence between population and authority framings is substantial, while divergence reflects positional framing rather than factual disagreement. The paper argues that such convergence, divergence, and silence are analytically meaningful in their own right, with direct implications for governance legitimacy, prevention strategies, and intervention feasibility in fragile contexts.

detail.abstract:
This Article examines the relationship between financial crises and regulatory frameworks that have failed to anticipate, contain, or adequately respond to emerging forms of market risk. It traces this problem from the speculative excesses preceding the 1929 stock market crash, through the deregulation and derivatives-driven vulnerabilities exposed by the 2008 financial crisis, to the continuing regulatory challenges illustrated by the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank. Across these episodes, a recurring concern emerges: financial innovation and speculative activity can develop more rapidly than the legal frameworks designed to supervise them, leaving regulators to respond after systemic risks have already materialized.

Against this historical background, the Article examines whether the existing federal regulatory framework is capable of addressing the rapidly expanding digital-asset and cryptocurrency markets. Particular attention is given to the continued application of the investment-contract doctrine established in SEC v. W.J. Howey Co., 328 U.S. 293 (1946), to financial instruments and transactions that were not contemplated when Howey was decided. The Article analyzes the jurisdictional difficulties faced by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in determining whether particular digital assets and transactions fall within existing securities or commodities laws. The resulting uncertainty raises fundamental questions concerning the allocation of regulatory authority, the treatment of digital-asset derivatives, and the adequacy of applying decades-old statutory and common-law concepts to rapidly evolving financial technology.

The Article argues that the central regulatory challenge is not simply whether digital assets should be regulated or exempted, but whether the existing federal framework can identify and address systemic risks before speculative activity becomes sufficiently interconnected to threaten broader financial stability. Drawing upon historical financial crises and contemporary digital-asset developments, this Article evaluates the limitations of relying primarily on judicial interpretation and broad statutory language to govern emerging financial markets. The analysis is limited to federal law and relevant common-law principles, including Howey, and does not address state Blue Sky laws.

detail.abstract:
We apply the Integrated Value (IV) framework of Schoenmaker and Schramade (2023) to 25 economically material ASX-listed non-financial companies, using inaugural FY2025 AASB S2 climate-related disclosures together with sustainability reports, regulatory filings, and public financial data at a common 30 June 2025 valuation date. For each firm we compute a Futureproofing Ratio (FR = 1 + TOR − TRR) that expresses monetised positive (TOR) and negative (TRR) social and environmental value flows relative to financial enterprise value. The study is deliberately positioned as a data-constrained measurement application: the intersection of mandate coverage, economic materiality, and usable disclosure is small in the first reporting year, and reporting dates, boundaries, and Scope 3 completeness remain heterogeneous. Two methodological contributions follow from those constraints — a tiered Scope 3 imputation procedure and a four-stream mining-waste classification that separates tailings and overburden from standard waste streams and prices each at distinct, institutionally grounded rates.

Under the maintained assumptions, the estimates show wide sectoral dispersion. The value-weighted FR is −2.029: gross negative externalities amount to approximately 4.05 times aggregate financial enterprise value and gross positive externalities to approximately 1.02 times, with the negative tail concentrated in coal, iron ore, hydrocarbons, and coal-fired generation, and the healthcare/technology group above unity. A ±50% sensitivity on the two novel mining-waste prices moves the value-weighted FR by less than 12% and leaves every firm ranking unchanged; rankings are also invariant, by construction, to the choice of social discount rate.

We then report an exploratory cross-sectional association between TRR and implied cost of equity. TRR and GLS-implied COE are positively rank-correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.608, p = 0.001, N = 25; ρ = 0.783 under an independent Yahoo Finance implementation), and the TRR coefficient is positive in all four OLS specifications. Under the paper’s pre-stated three-method rule (HC3 p < 0.05, FL-p < 0.05, and bootstrap CI excluding zero), no specification clears all three thresholds on the primary dataset: Spec 1 has HC3 p = 0.044 and bootstrap CI excluding zero, but FL-p = 0.055 exceeds the pre-stated threshold. We are explicit that this association cannot be separated at N = 25 from sector composition and book-to-market: removing the six Materials firms eliminates conventional significance, and asymptotic and bootstrap intervals in the full-control specifications include zero. The result is therefore presented as a directional consistency check that motivates — and does not substitute for — a pre-specified pooled DAX–AEX–ASX test. Implications for investors, superannuation trustees, and disclosure policy are drawn at the level the evidence supports.

Note on scope: The opportunity side of the FR (TOR) is reported in the measurement section and descriptive statistics but is excluded from all regressions. At N = 25, TOR's persistently positive coefficient reflects sector-composition confounds rather than a genuine opportunity signal; its regression analysis is deferred to the pooled DAX–AEX–ASX study.

detail.abstract: Certificate of Need (CON) laws require some types of health care facilities to demonstrate their economic necessity to a state board before opening or expanding. Every US state had a CON program at some point since 1980, and 34 currently maintain one. But the specific types of health facilities and equipment covered by CON vary immensely across states and time. Some states like Vermont require CON for as many as 27 separate types of health facilities, services, or equipment, including major ones like hospitals; while other states like Ohio require CON for only a single category like nursing homes. Due to data limitations, it has been common for research on CON to lump these all together as "CON states" and estimate a single treatment effect for CON programs as a whole. We introduce a new panel dataset on CON laws covering how 31 separate categories of health facilities and equipment were regulated in each state back to the 1980s. We describe the legal research process we used to find and categorize historical statutes in each state, and summarize trends in CON regulation. We suggest types of empirical research that may be enabled or improved by our data.

detail.abstract: This working paper argues that technical superiority is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for the diffusion of a new technology, and that the gap between technical capability and institutional readiness-the organizational, financial, and legal infrastructure required to convert an invention into a durable system-is a more reliable predictor of which technologies succeed. The argument is developed through a single historical case: the "War of the Currents" between Nikola Tesla's and George Westinghouse's alternating-current (AC) system and Thomas Edison's direct-current (DC) system, and the later collapse of Tesla's Wardenclyffe wireless-transmission project. Alternating current prevailed commercially despite Edison's better-funded opposition campaign, because Westinghouse supplied the institutional infrastructure-patent consolidation, standardization, capital access, and legal defense-that Tesla's invention alone could not provide. Wardenclyffe failed for the mirror-image reason: Tesla could not translate technical vision into a financing structure that J. P. Morgan and other investors could underwrite. The paper reframes this historical episode as an early instance of the institutional-readiness gap that the author's ongoing research program documents empirically in contemporary artificial-intelligence governance, and situates it explicitly alongside the author's related working papers on adaptation and human-capital readiness. The paper is conceptual and illustrative rather than causal: it draws on a single, well-documented historical case to motivate a framework, not to test it statistically.

detail.abstract:
This working paper develops a price-layer agenda linking injection technology—the incidence vector ω of monetary/fiscal inflows across assets and goods—to state-dependent comovement of an asset price index (API) and the CPI, under a medium-of-exchange (MoE) axiom. Relative purchasing power R=API/CPI is treated as an MoE diagnostic, not a third independent target. We reject unconditional level cointegration (H-level) as a headline prediction. Primary claims are H-price* (activity-orthogonal monetary residuals of API and CPI share a common factor) and H-ω (relative R responses track injection incidence under shared shocks).

On pre-registered US monthly S-primary 1987–2019 (excluding 2020–21), H-price* with INDPRO residualization yields equity–CPI residual correlation ≈0.411 (vs YoY ≈0.107). High-frequency Jarociński–Karadi monetary factors and Ramey–Zubairy defense-news fiscal shocks support a point-estimate ranking in which easing-equivalent monetary shocks raise cumulative Δln R at horizon 12 more than fiscal news (β≈0.1945 vs −0.0409); LOW transfer dummies replicate the order (β≈−0.146). Pre-registered continuous observational ω proxies give mixed results: Fed securities/GDP matches the asset-sign prediction weakly (β≈0.0367); transfers/DPI rejects the goods-sign prediction (β≈0.0484). v6.4 redefines goods/transfer ω toward check/rebate incidence and still rejects the continuous goods sign (EVENT Bush+ARRA weakly matches). Identification is labeled; rankings and observational ω fits are not structural causal proof. Primary H-price* evidence is S-primary F2* residual correlation (≈0.411), not full-sample correlation including 2020–21 (≈0.822). detail.title: Predicting adenosine fractional flow reserve from resting coronary pressure waveforms with deep sequence models: development, artifact quality control, and internal validation in the CONTRAST dataset
detail.abstract: Background and objective: We tested whether deep sequence models can predict adenosine fractional flow reserve (FFR) from resting coronary pressure recordings — avoiding adenosine hyperemia — and whether artifact quality control (QC) helps. Methods: From the public CONTRAST dataset (763 patients), an automated pipeline computed gold-standard adenosine FFR (within-event minimum smoothed beat-wise Pd/Pa), anchored against core-lab figures. Deep sequence models (CNN, BiLSTM, Transformer; 10 s plateau-anchored Pa/Pd windows) underwent patient-level 5-fold cross-validation against resting Pd/Pa, iFR, contrast FFR (cFFR), and gradient boosting; primary endpoint: mean absolute error (MAE), paired bootstrap. A Fit5Mega-trained (2485 patients) artifact-QC module was tested in- and cross-domain; all endpoints were repeated under an event-mean label. Results: 437 patients had a usable label (75.3% FFR ≤ 0.80). Transformer MAE 0.0941 [0.0866–0.1024] beat all baselines; on the dual-label subset (n = 275) the cFFR advantage (ΔMAE -0.0172) survived Holm correction, but discrimination (AUC 0.7414) did not exceed cFFR (p = 0.111) and varied across seeds (0.654–0.757; MAE stable). Under an event-mean label, prevalence fell to 56.8%, MAE to 0.0362 (AUC 0.8931), while the advantage over cFFR (published definition) lost significance (p = 0.156). Re-weighted to 47% cath-lab prevalence, positive predictive value fell to 0.51 (negative predictive value 0.82). QC transfer was null (ρ = 0.0048). Conclusion: Deep sequence models estimate adenosine FFR from resting waveforms more accurately than all resting indices; the contrast-FFR advantage is definition-dependent and predictive values at clinical prevalence modest. External, core-lab-anchored validation is required; the artifact-QC module did not transfer across sensor domains.

detail.abstract:
Archaeological evidence from the public squares of ancient Rome and Pompeii reveals that graffiti in those forums regularly carried false political statements and demeaning claims about women, a striking parallel to social media today. This Article examines how Roman law likely addressed injurious public speech, from the Lex Aquilia's penalties for property damage to the actio iniuriarum (injury action), which protected a person's corpus (body), fama (reputation), and dignitas (dignity). Roman law made it possible for authorities to remove graffiti and levy fines or corporally punish offenders, treating attacks on reputation and dignity as legally cognizable injuries nearly 2,000 years before modern personality rights emerged. 

The Article then turns to the digital public square, where the proliferation of deepfake pornography and AI-generated sexual imagery raises strikingly questions. It argues that so-called "personality rights" are not a novel legal development but a resurgence of protections that Roman law, rooted in ius naturale, had already extended to the "inner self." Roman authorities could act immediately to vindicate them, in contrast to today's still-unsettled debates over dignity in the digital sphere.

detail.abstract: Constitutional doctrines governing the relationship between the state and religion routinely adjudicate disputes that turn on metaphysical claims-the existence of God, the truth of a creation account, the authenticity of a spiritual experience-without ever purporting to resolve those claims. This article asks how constitutional adjudication performs that operation, and argues that it does so through what this article calls an epistemic proxy: an institutional criterion substituted for a truth inquiry that the adjudicator is structurally unable to conduct. Using a vertical reading of the demarcation criteria applied to intelligent design in Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District alongside a horizontal comparison of religion-state doctrine in the United States, France, Germany, Brazil, and India, the article shows that every mature secularism regime performs the same underlying suspension of judgment on metaphysical truth, yet operationalizes that suspension through structurally different proxies-purpose inquiry, historical practice and tradition, formal separation, state neutrality, and basic-structure secularism, respectively. The choice of proxy, rather than the formal degree of separation between religion and state, is shown to determine how the burden of justificatory doubt is distributed between religious and nonreligious citizens. The article traces this proxy logic to the ordinary law of evidence, arguing that constitutional agnosticism is best understood as a graduated, jurisdiction-specific analogue to burden-of-proof allocation rather than as a fixed ideological commitment to secularism or religion. It examines the leading counterargument-that facially neutral proxies such as historical-practice review can themselves reintroduce majoritarian truth judgments by privileging the metaphysical claims that happen to be historically dominant-and proposes a modest interpretive heuristic, proxy disclosure, under which courts are asked to identify explicitly which epistemic proxy they are applying and why, rather than migrating silently between proxies to reach a preferred result. The article's contribution is doctrinal and theoretical rather than empirical: it does not propose a new constitutional right, but a vocabulary for describing an operation that comparative constitutional law already performs but has not yet named. detail.abstract: Matter changes what it does at particular values of the energetic conditions imposed on it, and those values differ between materials while the conditions imposing them do not. This paper proposes that the parameter along which the values are ordered is a property of the radiation field rather than of matter. Two bodies sharing no boundary and exchanging no particles still equilibrate, and radiation is the only channel available to them; Kirchhoff's relation, which follows from the second law, fixes spectral emissivity equal to spectral absorptivity and makes the equilibrium spectral function universal, with material identity entering only through the coupling coefficients. A criterion separates switching from response: at a switching threshold the state, symmetry, pathway or governing mechanism changes, which the Landau expansion shows need not require a discontinuous observable. Each material carries an ordered threshold set while the index on which all sets are inscribed is shared. For ordinary molecular and condensed-matter processes the electronic modes supply the principal interface through which radiation reshapes the potential surface governing nuclear configuration, by the Born-Oppenheimer separation. Radiation switches matter without thermalisation at the photoelectric cutoff, the semiconductor absorption edge, inner-shell edges and in photoisomerisation, and the conservation of orbital symmetry establishes that the mode of radiative input selects the reaction pathway and not only its rate. A cross-field kinetic calculation is examined as an instance of parameter collapse. Falsification conditions are stated, including the unresolved case of zero-temperature quantum criticality.

detail.abstract: This article evaluates the strategic case for millennial retirement portfolios to incorporate long-term U.S. Treasuries, framing the current high-yield environment as a historic "generational entry point." Bypassing conventional market consensus, the study uses independent historical datasets from the Federal Reserve and Yahoo Finance spanning from 1962 to 2026. The findings validate Bank of America’s macro thesis that long-term Treasuries have suffered an unprecedented rolling 10-year annualized loss of roughly negative 2%, creating an exhausted valuation profile mirroring historic asset market troughs. The normalization of the yield curve to above 5% and real 10-year yields peaking over 1% fundamentally correct the unfavorable duration risk asymmetry observed during the pandemic’s ultra-low rate regime. The paper provides actionable implementations for a $100,000 fixed-income allocation by analyzing two distinct ETF structures: a pure core defined-maturity ladder and a hybrid ladder with long-duration satellites (TLT and ZROZ). Scenario stress tests and risk mitigation analyses demonstrate how these structures automate reinvestment cycles, lock in predictable cash flows, and cushion portfolios against asymmetric interest-rate shocks.

detail.abstract: This chapter adapts Kalecki’s profit equation to the post-war British national accounts. In particular, it examines the secular decline in the profit share between the early 1960s and 1970s that exercised both government and academic observers at the time. Using a sequence of national accounts identities, it demonstrates that the profit share started to fall in the 1960s when the company sector's share of value added in GDP started to fall, despite the share of company investment in GDP increasing throughout the post-war period. The counterpart to this process was the public sector increasing in size. Meanwhile, non-profit income flows increased between the 1960s and 1970s, and then exploded in the 1980s. Despite these changes, company sector disposable income and net fixed capital formation were remarkably stable over the second half of the twentieth century.

detail.abstract: Liquidity is a necessary precondition for orderly markets, facilitating trading, price discovery, and shock absorption. Unlike traditional financial markets, where liquidity is supported by a cohort of regulated institutions, clearinghouses, and central banks, digital asset market liquidity relies on specialized intermediaries whose participation is discretionary and highly pro-cyclical. This Article shows that-despite the avowedly decentralized and disintermediated nature of digital asset markets-they depend on a cohort of intermediaries for their function. This Article provides the first study of these digital asset market makers (DAMMs). It identifies, categorizes, and analyzes the actors that sustain liquidity across centralized and decentralized venues. Drawing on handcollected data on fifty-two major DAMMs, it provides the first systematic account of digital asset market making as a distinct and systemically significant market function. The Article shows that market making is foundational to efficient digital assets markets: when liquidity providers withdraw, price discovery deteriorates, volatility accelerates, and trading can become disorderly-dynamics starkly revealed by the October 2025 digital asset liquidation event. Although DAMMs perform the same core economic function as traditional market makers-continuous liquidity provision-they operate through technology-native business models that combine centralized and decentralized infrastructures, off-chain contractual arrangements, and onchain protocols. These innovations broaden access to liquidity and reduce frictions under normal conditions, but they also introduce new forms of opacity, pro-cyclicality, and market fragility during stress. Current regulatory frameworks-organized around more traditional notions of exchanges and traders-are ill-suited to address the risks and organizational structure and practices of DAMMs. In response, this Article advances a functional-and-structural approach that defines DAMMs broadly to include any professional liquidity provider whose activity materially shapes market outcomes. It proposes an ex-ante notification-based supervisory regime, complemented by supervisory technology (the use of innovative technology by supervisory agencies) to enable near-real-time monitoring of assets, blockchains, and smart contracts while preserving innovation and competition. By treating liquidity provision as a core object of regulation rather than a peripheral trading activity, this approach strengthens market integrity, investor protection, and financial stability in an increasingly crossborder and technologically complex digital asset ecosystem.

detail.abstract: I examine how the March 2025 implementation of Fixed Income Clearing Corporation (FICC) customer-margin segregation and enhanced access models affects the conditional distribution of U.S. Treasury repo spreads. Using daily observations from 2023 to 2026, I estimate conditional quantile regressions following Koenker and Bassett (1978) on the secured funding spread between the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) and the Interest on Reserve Balances rate (IORB). My central premise is that the effects of clearing need not be uniform across funding conditions. For dealer intermediaries, greater multilateral netting can reduce effective balance-sheet usage and compress funding spreads. At the same time, tighter collateral and margin requirements can increase financing costs when intermediary capacity is scarce. Consistent with these offsetting forces, the estimated clearing-related effect is negative at the median (β 0.50 =-2.29 bps, p < 0.001) but reverses sign in the upper tail, reaching +3.12 bps at τ = 0.90 (p < 0.001). I also find pronounced heterogeneity in quarter-end effects associated with Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) constraints, with the estimated spread increase rising from +7.18 bps at τ = 0.10 to +14.55 bps at τ = 0.90. The results suggest that the incidence of Treasury repo funding frictions is state dependent: the potential benefits of netting are more visible in the center of the distribution, while collateral and balance-sheet constraints become increasingly important in the upper tail.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the contemporaneous association between security returns and accounting earnings under various combinations of three innovations, that have been previously considered but separately studied in prior work on the return earnings relationship: (i) employing the current level of earnings, together with the change in earnings as a proxy for unexpected earnings, (ii) distinguishing between permanent versus transitory earnings and (iii) isolating positive from negative earnings. detail.abstract: Previous UK evidence on the value relevance of accounting information over time is scarce. Therefore, this study evaluates whether the value relevance of accounting information has changed over time in UK firms. Specifically, based on UK data, this study examines whether the value relevance of earnings, cash flows and book values has become less value relevant. To examine whether the value relevance of earnings, cash flows and book values has changed over time, we employ a regression of the annual adjusted R-squared values and response coefficients (of the association between capital market variables and accounting information) on a time trend variable. The value relevance is said to have decreased (increased) over time if the estimated time coefficient is significantly negative (positive). The results show that the value relevance of earnings, cash flows, and earnings and book values together is unchanged over the investigated period. Moreover, the general conclusion of unchanged value relevance over time remains the same for large firms when compared to small firms. These results are robust to controlling for the extremity of earnings and cash flows, and industry sectors. Therefore, the claim of a decline over time in the value relevance of accounting information is not supported by the empirical evidence. Our results show that the value relevance of accounting information is unchanged. This study contributes to the scarce UK research on changes over time in the value relevance of accounting information.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the concept and measurement of national wealth and distinguishes wealth from GDP and capital stock. It argues that GDP measures current economic production rather than the accumulated wealth of a nation. Using the United Kingdom as a case study, the paper considers major components of national wealth, including physical and financial capital, human capital, natural resources, land, businesses, infrastructure, government assets, transportation assets, and net foreign assets. Based on available 2024 estimates, the study produces a preliminary estimate of approximately £38.45 trillion for UK national wealth, compared with GDP of approximately £2.905 trillion. The findings suggest that national wealth is a broader measure of a country's accumulated economic resources and productive capacity than GDP alone.

detail.abstract:
Background and Aims: The National Drug and Alcohol Treatment Monitoring System (NDTMS) is England’s national administrative dataset for publicly commissioned structured drug and alcohol treatment. Although widely used for surveillance, its use for research has not been well characterised. We aimed to characterise the extent and development of NDTMS-based research, compare substantive and methodological coverage between routine surveillance and non-routine analysis, and describe data linkage, research access, and collaboration.

Methods: We conducted a scoping review of NDTMS-based research from 2005 onwards, following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-Scoping Review guidance. Bibliographic databases, grey literature sources, and citation searching were used to identify eligible outputs. Searches were completed in July 2026. We mapped substantive and methodological coverage, data linkage, and reported routes of access, distinguishing recurring surveillance from non-routine analysis. Bibliometric analyses characterised the peer reviewed literature.

Results: We included 83 outputs: 45 journal articles, 34 governmental outputs, and four doctoral theses. Twenty-eight (33.7%) were recurring national surveillance outputs, and 55 (66.3%) were non-routine analyses. Among non-routine outputs, 51 (92.7%) included adults, 45 (81.8%) opioids, and 39 (70.9%) alcohol, compared with 14 (25.5%) including children or young people and six (10.9%) secure-setting populations. Twenty-five outputs (30.1%) used external individual-level linkage, most commonly with criminal justice, mortality, prison/probation, and hospital data. Among 51 non-governmental outputs, a specific route of access was reported for 31 (60.8%), with multiple national, local, and project-specific arrangements. The 45 journal articles involved 141 authors, of whom 35 contributed to at least two included articles.

Summary: Routine surveillance using England’s National Drug and Alcohol Treatment Monitoring System has covered a broader range of populations and substances than dedicated analytic research, which has concentrated on adult opioid and alcohol treatment. Individual-level linkage has extended research to outcomes beyond treatment services; clearer, proportionate access through secure research environments and reusable linkage pathways could broaden the range of researchers and questions supported by these data.

detail.title: Time Use and Population Representation in the Sloan Study of Adolescents
detail.abstract: Do studies of time use interfere too much in the lives of the subjects?  As a result are those who agree to participate a biased sample of the population?  We examine the characteristics of the Experience Sampling Method (ESM) adolescent sample from the Alfred P. Sloan Study of Youth and Social Development in order to detect and quantify instances of sampling and nonresponse bias.  According to available proxies for time use and standard demographic variables, the Sloan ESM sample is nearly representative in terms of teen employment rates, parental employment rates, a student's grade point average, and TV watching.  Work hours are slightly undercounted in the study because of slightly higher nonresponse rates by teenagers working long hours.  The sample is less representative in terms of the time of week and gender; nonresponse is relatively common on school nights and (to a lesser extent) on weekends, and among boys.  We offer some suggestions regarding general implications of our findings for the measurement of time use.

title: Can the Doha Round be a Development Round? Setting a Place at the Table
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics and Stanford University

detail.title: Can the Doha Round be a Development Round? Setting a Place at the Table
detail.abstract: A fundamental objective of the Doha Round of WTO negotiations is to improve the trading prospects of developing countries. The 2001 declaration from the WTO Ministerial Conference in Doha, Qatar, commits the member governments to negotiations aimed at substantial improvements in market access with a view to phasing out export subsidies, while embracing "special and differential treatment" for developing countries as an integral part of all elements of the negotiations. The main message of this paper comes in three parts. First, these stated aims are incompatible from the perspective of our economic analysis; thus, if these aims are pursued as stated, then we conclude that they are unlikely to deliver the meaningful trade gains for developing countries that the WTO membership seeks. Second, in attempting to integrate its developing country membership into the world trading system, the WTO may face a "latecomers" problem that, while occurring also in earlier rounds, is unprecedented in its scale in the Doha Round, and which could potentially account for the current impasse. And third, we argue that if the Round maintains its stated aims but moves away from the non-reciprocal special-and-differential treatment norm as the cornerstone of the approach to meeting developing country needs in the WTO, and if developing countries prepare, in markets where they are large, to come to the bargaining table and to negotiate reciprocally with each other and with developing nations, then it might be possible to break the impasse at Doha, to address the latecomers problem, and to deliver trade gains for developing countries.

detail.abstract: This essay explores the Ontario Tobacco Research Unit's Review of Canada's tobacco Endgame strategy, that aims to reduce smoking to 5% of the population by 2035. That Review sees new generation nicotine products as a problem rather than as a solution to smoking and smoking-related deaths and subsumes those lower risk products into the 5% goal. This is both unrealistic and unnecessary. The evidence produced in the Review on policies adopted in other jurisdictions is incomplete and selective and ignores important literature. Unreasonable and unnecessary goals are socially disruptive.

detail.abstract: Between 1982 and 2013 the Islamic Azad University, a tuition-charging private system, opened branches in 285 of Iran's 397 counties, bringing college within reach of provincial towns while leaving tuition in place. This paper uses the staggered timing of these openings, matched to the 2 percent microdata of the 2016 and 2011 censuses, to ask who gained when college came to town. Comparing birth cohorts within counties with a Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator on a countyby-cohort panel, the paper finds that a local branch raised tertiary completion by about 4 to 5 percentage points among cohorts who grew up with it, on a base of 12 to 20 percent. The gain is a women's gain: men show no effect. It is larger for residents of the county town than for rural residents, although that difference is less precisely estimated. The same branches raise the share of young women who remain unmarried, and the share living with their parents, by 7 to 9 points. Exploratory evidence on family background points in one direction: children of more educated parents and households with more assets show the larger gains, and educational persistence across generations is not lower in treated counties. The pattern is consistent with a gender difference in the geographic constraint on college attendance; whether the money constraint also bound, and for whom, the data cannot establish.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of identifiable smooth ambiguity in a finite-state Anscombe-Aumann framework in which ambiguity perception and the ambiguity-attitude representation may depend on the act's endogenous certainty-equivalent utility level. The framework separates two sources of utility-level dependence that standard smooth-ambiguity models hold fixed. Neutral-transfer experiments within revealed cells recover conditional beliefs, while compensation experiments across cells recover cell weights and locally revealed ambiguity attitude scales. These objects have distinct behavioral content. After the within-level structure is extended globally, ambiguity perception is identified at each certainty-equivalent level, whereas variation in admissible level-specific global attitude indices need not by itself reflect behaviorally identified variation in ambiguity attitude. Cross-level restrictions determine when the locally revealed attitude scales can instead be represented by one common global ambiguity-attitude index. The baseline characterization yields a doubly implicit smooth-ambiguity representation with level-specific perception and potentially level specific global attitude indices. Requiring one common ambiguity-attitude index gives an intermediate stable-attitude model in which only perception may vary; imposing perception stability as well yields standard identifiable smooth ambiguity within the maintained full support, neutrally separated, fixed-partition environment with at least three revealed cells. The contribution is therefore a behavioral decomposition of utility-level dependence in smooth ambiguity into separately revealed perception and attitude components.

title: Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall: Measuring Tail Risk in a Technology Equity Portfolio

detail.abstract:
This paper applies Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (CVaR) to a portfolio of
four large-cap tech stocks: Apple (AAPL), Alphabet/Google (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and
NVIDIA (NVDA). I pulled the actual daily price data from Yahoo Finance using the yfinance
Python library with auto_adjust=True, which automatically corrects for stock splits and
dividends so that each return reflects what an investor actually experienced. The data covers
January 2, 2022 through December 31, 2024, giving 751 trading days.
I chose this three-year window deliberately because it covers three structurally different market
environments: the 2022 tech selloff, the 2023 recovery driven by AI, and the 2024 extended
rally. Having all three in the same dataset makes the risk estimates more realistic and more
robust than if I had only looked at a single market regime.
The method I used is historical simulation. You sort the actual historical returns and read off the
loss at a given quantile, without assuming any particular distribution. This is the most intuitive
approach, and it is also widely used in practice because it captures the heavy tails and skewness
that are present in real financial return data, especially for tech stocks.
I chose an equally weighted portfolio to isolate the effect of diversification and risk measurement
without introducing bias from a specific optimization strategy. Each stock receives a 25%
weight, representing $25,000 each within a $100,000 portfolio.
For this portfolio, the 1-day VaR at 95% confidence comes out to $3,139.14. That means on
about one out of every 20 trading days (roughly 5% of the time), you’d expect to lose more than
that amount. I also computed the Expected Shortfall (CVaR), which tells you how bad losses
actually are on average on those worst days. At 95%, that number is $4,101.54, about 31% above
the VaR threshold.
That gap is the most important finding in this paper: VaR tells you where the threshold is, while
CVaR shows how severe losses actually are once that threshold is crossed. In a tech-heavy
portfolio, that difference has significant implications for risk management.
The paper also breaks down the VaR for each individual $25,000 position, where NVDA alone
carries nearly twice the tail risk of AAPL or MSFT. I also look at the diversification benefit you
get from holding all four stocks together rather than treating each position separately, which
comes out to $356.81, roughly a 10% reduction in risk.
Finally, I extend the 1-day estimates to a 10-day horizon using the square-root-of-time rule,
giving a 95% VaR of $9,926.83, which is consistent with Basel II and Basel III reporting
frameworks. The limitations of historical simulation are discussed openly in the final section.

detail.abstract: Financial systems are becoming continuous faster than investor context is becoming continuous. Tokenized securities can move across new market rails and representations, U.S. equity markets are preparing for longer operating windows, and artificial intelligence systems are progressing from recommendation toward multi-step action. Yet many investor-facing decisions still rely on a state of the investor, portfolio and authorization framework captured at an earlier point in time. This paper introduces Decision Half-Life as a research construct for measuring how long the context underlying a financial decision remains sufficiently valid before a material change requires revalidation. It develops three related concepts: Context Decay, where accurate information loses decision relevance as facts change; Authority Drift, where an automated system remains technically authorized while the factual context supporting the action has changed; and Decision Replayability, where a supervisor can reconstruct the state, evidence, material change, authority boundary, human intervention and outcome after an event. The framework is designed for the convergence of tokenized securities, near-continuous market infrastructure and agentic investment workflows. It separates asset and infrastructure revalidation from investor-context revalidation, proposes a technology-neutral control loop based on detection, selective revalidation, escalation and preserved evidence, and establishes an empirical programme for measuring detection latency, material-event recall, alert burden, authority drift and replay completeness. NeuFin's current research environment provides an initial instrumentation base for this work, including market events, portfolio positions, regime observations, audit records, market snapshots and decision records with fields for priority, suitability findings, evidence, data quality and human review. The paper's central argument is that time is becoming a first-class dimension of decision assurance: the question is no longer only whether a decision was authorized or well-supported when it began, but whether the context supporting it remains materially valid when action occurs.

title: Financing Decisions and Product Introductions of Private and Publicly Traded Firms
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and

detail.title: Financing Decisions and Product Introductions of Private and Publicly Traded Firms
detail.abstract: We exploit Medicare national coverage reimbursement approvals of medical devices as a quasi-natural experiment to investigate how private and publicly traded firm financing decisions and product introductions respond to exogenous changes in investment opportunities. We find that publicly traded companies increase their external financing, and their subsequent product introductions, by more than private companies in response to national coverage approvals.  The primary source of the increased financing is through private financing of public firms. We also show that firms that select to go public during our sample period are ex ante more productive than similar private firms.  The results are consistent with public firms bearing the costs of going public to gain financing advantages that come from being able to offer securities with better exit liquidity and lower price risk.

detail.abstract:
Science-based startups in Latin America, and globally, face a structural challenge that existing innovation frameworks do not adequately address: the transition from a new scientific function to a new competitive market category. The literature on exaptation in business contexts explains how preexisting capabilities migrate to new functions. The category design tradition explains how new markets are named, positioned, and dominated. Neither explains what happens in between,the interval during which a new function exists but a new category has not yet formed, and during which the decisions made by founders, investors, and ecosystem builders determine whether the innovation achieves categorical significance or stalls as a functional curiosity.

This paper introduces the Theory of Exaptive Innovation and Competitive Category Formation: a middle-range theory that maps the full arc from scientific capability to new competitive category through a seven-link exaptive chain, identifies the conditions under which each transition in the chain occurs or fails, and generates operational tools for the practitioners who need to navigate it. Drawing on evolutionary biology, the economics of new markets, cognitive neuroscience, and the philosophy of emergent innovation, the theory establishes that the transition from new function to new category requires collective recognition, active niche construction, and the crossing of a threshold this paper calls the moment of non-comparison. Three longitudinal cases, Corning's development of optical fiber, Beeflow's construction of managed pollination intelligence, and Ginkgo Bioworks' trajectory of sequential exaptation and ongoing categorical repositioning, illustrate the chain at different stages and degrees of completion. Implications are developed for science-based founders, investors, company builders, and the designers of scientific innovation ecosystems.

detail.abstract: The increasing borderlessness of crypto-asset markets presents a structural challenge to regulatory systems that remain predominantly territorial. This paper asks whether crossborder crypto-asset activity can be governed through nationally confined regulatory frameworks or requires internationally coordinated minimum standards. Using a comparative, doctrinal and interdisciplinary method, it analyses India, the United Kingdom, the European Union and Singapore alongside materials from the FSB, FATF, IMF, IOSCO and BIS. It distinguishes regulatory diversity, competition, arbitrage and evasion, and develops the concept of an accessibility-enforcement gap: a service that is readily accessible to users in one jurisdiction while remaining difficult for that jurisdiction's authorities to supervise or enforce against. The paper proposes the International Crypto-Asset Regulatory Floor (ICARF) as a model of regulatory interoperability rather than uniformity. ICARF comprises six pillars with minimum outcomes and mutual-recognition criteria; a soft-law-plus core with an optional, separately constituted oversight tier whose legal basis is stated rather than assumed; a threshold model of adoption incentives with an explicit tipping point; and a treatment of decentralized finance, self-custody and stable coin issuers, which the intermediary-based pillars cannot reach on their own. An appendix presents an illustrative Offshore Exposure Gap Index (OEGI) for eight jurisdictions, with a sensitivity analysis, a cross-check against FATF's July 2026 implementation data, and coded legal-perimeter and enforcement indicators for five jurisdictions. The paper makes no causal empirical claims. The OEGI is an author-constructed scoring rubric, not an official statistic, and ICARF is a hypothesis, not an existing standard. The central argument is that effective international crypto-asset regulation need not require a single global regulator or identical national laws. Compatible minimum outcomes, recognized through credible peer review and market-access incentives, can allow different legal systems to interoperate in a borderless market.

title: Do Women Ask for Less? The Gender Ask Gap in Science Funding

detail.abstract: Research funding shapes which scientific questions get pursued and at what scale, making access to grants one of the most consequential forces in a research career. Women receive fewer and smaller grants than men across many fields, an inequality that may compound over time and steer science away from the questions women are more likely to ask. Most research has examined gender gaps in grant success rates, but the amount a researcher ultimately receives depends not only on their probability of being awarded funding, but also on how much they request in the first place, a stage that has rarely been observed directly. Here, we show, using application-level records from two large European philanthropic science funders, that women request substantially less funding than comparable men. Controlling for applicant track record, proposal quality as assessed by external reviewers, and fixed effects for funder, grant type, university, and subfield, we find that women request 5.4 per cent less at the proposal stage-a gap that accounts for roughly three-quarters of the well-known gap in funding awarded. Making a smaller request does not improve the odds of success, so the gap does not reflect a winning strategy. Instead, we find that the gap is largest among more junior and less experienced researchers and narrows as researchers apply repeatedly, pointing to differences in experience rather than project scope. Despite receiving less, women produce as much research from each grant as men, yet their smaller awards result in the formation of smaller teams that constrain the broader output sustaining scientific careers. These findings relocate a central source of inequality in science from how proposals are judged to how they are constructed.

detail.abstract: Current economic arrangements lack the boundary conditions necessary for systemic stability. This paper argues that a Floor and Ceiling on resource distribution are structural necessities, prior to ethics or politics, for any productive system with interdependent participants. Production is the physical basis of human existence and requires balancing loops to remain viable, as every sustainable system in nature demonstrates. The Floor maintains the consumption base necessary for production to continue-a systemcontinuity condition, not a poverty measure-grounded both in functional necessity and in the prior claim of every participant on the collectively produced surplus; its design must also account for the documented psychological functions of structured activity, not income alone, with the balance between unconditional and participation-based models left to democratic deliberation. The Ceiling prevents self-reinforcing concentration from consuming the system that generated it. Its necessary form is a hard limit rather than steeply progressive taxation alone: where the return on capital persistently exceeds economic growth, a tax that only slows accumulation still permits it to continue without bound, and only an absolute limit guarantees the bounded state a balancing loop requires. Between these boundaries, markets operate freely within the space the boundary conditions define. The paper positions this account against the ethical and political traditions of distribution theory, against its closest structural predecessor, Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics, and against the cornucopian claim that human ingenuity dissolves the need for any boundary at all-arguing that this last objection does not reach the Floor, and that the empirical record on market concentration and innovation runs against it where it does reach the Ceiling. The Ceiling's durability, in turn, depends less on the legal instrument than on a structurally literate citizenry able to recognize and resist capture attempts as they arise. Accelerating automation makes the whole argument more urgent by weakening the wage channel that has historically supplied both income and structured purpose together. This paper offers a theoretical starting point, not an implementation blueprint; specific forms will evolve through democratic deliberation within each society.

detail.title: Transfer Study of Scene Text Removal Models for Multimodality DICOM Image Anonymization using Synthetic Data
detail.abstract: The Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format is widely used to store medical images along with patient-related Protected Health Information (PHI) within hospital Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). However, the compliant anonymization of DICOM objects for PACS-to-PACS transmission remains challenging. Our objective is to identify a lightweight conditioned Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) adapted from Scene Text Removal (STR) models, capable of effectively removing burned-in text from DICOM images while restoring the underlying tissue structures. To this aim, we generated a synthetic dataset with 620 images from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) database, containing four modalities with fake PHI. A localized generation strategy is applied to minimize unintended errors outside the burned-in text regions, as they typically occupy only a small portion. Then, five cGAN-based architectures are fine-tuned and compared to evaluate their reconstruction performance, FLOPs and inference time. After fine-tuning, all models are subsequently evaluated on CPU-only inference to assess their real-world transferability, identifying GaRNet model as the best trade-off across different evaluation aspects. Compared with the second-best cGAN, MTRNet++, GaRNet required 23.6 times fewer FLOPs and achieved 11.4 times faster inference while maintaining comparable structural similarity and PSNR score.

detail.abstract: This study examines how working from home (WFH) shapes time allocation, divisions of labor, and subjective time pressure within dual-earner couples. Using high-quality longitudinal panel data from Australian couples, we analyse the joint effects of partners’ WFH arrangements, distinguishing impacts by intensity and frequency of home-based work. Results from family fixed-effect models reveal that short-hours WFH is associated with increased paid work for both partners, higher total workloads, and elevated time stress. In contrast, high-intensity WFH redistributes unpaid labour more equitably when men work from home, modestly alleviating women’s time pressure, but is largely concentrated among men with high job autonomy. Gendered effects are pronounced: women’s workloads and time stress respond to both their own and their partner’s WFH, whereas men’s outcomes are largely unaffected by their partner’s arrangements. Overall, WFH does not systematically narrow gender gaps in couples; its effects depend critically on relative WFH intensity between partners.

detail.abstract: This paper provides an empirical, post-implementation assessment of the trade effects of the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Using monthly bilateral trade data for 20 major non-EU exporting economies and six destination markets (the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Australia, and Canada) over the period January 2016 to mid-2026, the paper employs a difference-indifferences framework that exploits the sectoral boundaries of CBAM coverage to identify the causal effect of the mechanism on export volumes. Two complementary specifications are estimated. The first shows that exports of products proposed for inclusion under the 2028 downstream expansion of CBAM (S2 products) rose significantly relative to a matched control group following the onset of the CBAM transitional phase in October 2023, consistent with a pre-emptive export surge.
