detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence systems move from generating outputs to executing multi-step workflows, the control problem shifts from response quality to delegated action. This paper proposes the delegation contract, a six-field task-level framework for agentic AI that integrates semantic task specification with operational authority and escalation. A delegation contract specifies objective, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, authority, and escalation. The first four fields define semantic delegation: what the task means and how acceptable completion will be recognized. The final two define operational delegation: what the agent may do and when decision rights must return to another actor.

The framework is positioned relative to principal-agent theory, meaningful human control, authenticated delegation, agent infrastructure, authorization architectures, and contemporary agent governance. Its contribution is integrative rather than a claim that the individual elements are new: it treats purpose, completion evidence, delegated action rights, and return-of-control conditions as one coherent task-level control object.

The paper also outlines characteristic failure modes, a lightweight machine-readable implementation pattern, risk-adjusted specification depth, and authority attenuation in multi-agent delegation. The central claim is that reliable agentic autonomy requires more than a clear prompt and more than scoped permissions; it requires an explicit specification of what counts as success, what the agent is authorized to do, and when that authority expires.

detail.abstract: Digital image steganography constitutes a vital pillar of covert communications and privacy-preserving data transmission. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical formulation, technical implementation, and empirical evaluation of Least Significant Bit (LSB) substitution within 24-bit uncompressed Bitmap (BMP) cover images. The study details the binary architecture of the 54-byte BMP header, formulates exact mathematical models for multi-bit plane replacement, and derives closed-form expressions for payload capacity limits and spatial distortion metrics including Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM). A full three-tier software application developed in C# .NET is evaluated across high-entropy carrier media, demonstrating that 1-bit LSB substitution achieves exceptional visual fidelity (>52 dB PSNR) while hiding up to 369 KB of encrypted binary payloads within standard test carriers. Furthermore, a rigorous steganalysis vulnerability analysis is performed, focusing on Chi-Square (χ²) histogram distribution attacks alongside a review of contemporary anti-forensic developments, establishing spatial LSB steganography as both a robust baseline and a foundational reference for modern covert data hiding research.

detail.abstract: Hospitals deploy digital navigation to reduce frictions in outpatient care with an expectation that better navigation will shorten patient journey duration. However, when patients themselves execute parts of the care process, digital navigation may change when they enter and which activities they undertake, potentially lengthening journey duration. We examine this tension in a large-scale field experiment involving 850,947 patients at a major hospital. Patients were randomly assigned access to digital navigation guiding them throughout outpatient visit. Take-up was only 3%, limiting the impact of deployment. However, among patients induced to use digital navigation by randomized access, journey duration increased by 93 minutes. The longer duration reflected two changes: patients checked in earlier and were less likely to be late for scheduled consultations, while undertaking more laboratory tests and report printing. Diagnostic examinations did not increase, a pattern consistent with scheduling constraints limiting immediate action. We show that digital navigation can reshape how patients execute multistage service processes and that its realized effects depend on both adoption and whether patients can act on the information provided. Accordingly, shorter journey duration may not be the right benchmark for evaluating digital navigation.

detail.abstract: Students entering the management workforce now have to think about more than a résumé. In many cases, a recruiter, alumnus, or potential employer can encounter a candidate through LinkedIn or another digital platform before any formal interview takes place. This has created a strong culture of professional visibility: students are encouraged to post, network, build a personal brand, and make their achievements visible. But an important question is often left out of that conversation: does being visible all the time actually help? This paper examines that question through the concepts of digital silence and strategic online minimalism. Digital silence refers to limited public professional activity online, while strategic online minimalism refers to a deliberate choice to maintain enough professional information and connectivity to remain discoverable without continuously sharing content. The distinction matters because online visibility can create opportunities, but it can also create privacy concerns, reputational exposure, and pressure to remain constantly active. The paper reviews published research on LinkedIn, professional identity, social-media recruitment, digital networking, cybervetting, and employability. Existing evidence suggests that professional digital platforms can support career development and networking, while research also shows that users and recruiters are concerned with privacy, fairness, and the quality of online information. Particularly relevant to the Indian context, a recent study of 223 final-year university students examined attitudes toward cybervetting and found LinkedIn to be perceived as the most acceptable and fair platform among the platforms studied. A separate 2026 study of 93 business-management students found relationships between LinkedIn-related attitudes, career interest, career prospects, and industry commitment. Rather than arguing that students should become either highly visible or completely silent, this paper proposes a middle position: professional visibility should be purposeful. The paper develops a conceptual model in which strategic online minimalism influences professional digital visibility, which may influence online social capital and professional opportunity exposure, ultimately contributing to perceived employability. The paper concludes with hypotheses and a research design that can be tested using primary data. No original survey findings are claimed.

detail.abstract: AI-moderated interviews are emerging as a scalable market-research method for generating consumer insights and building consumer "digital twins." Yet it remains unclear whether they match human-moderated interviews or improve on simpler, static data collection methods. In a pre-registered, between-subjects study (𝑁 = 317) with three industry partners, we compare AI-moderated (𝑁 = 154), human-moderated (𝑁 = 24), and static interviews (𝑁 = 154). AI moderation matches human moderation in depth, covers more themes, and, holding budget constant, recovers significantly more customer needs than human moderation or static interviews. However, participants sound more emotionally engaged when speaking to a live human. We then create digital twins using interview data and evaluate each twin against the participant's own held-out responses to six real-world marketing stimuli. We find that digital twins created from AI-moderated interviews predict consumer responses better than demographics-only personas. However, the additional richness from AI moderation does not translate into better quantitative predictions compared to static interviews. By analyzing open-ended thoughts generated from humans versus their twins, we find that prediction errors are connected both to differences in (self-reported) thinking styles between twins and humans, and to gaps between training and validation data (i.e., asking questions that are too far out of distribution).

title: Educating like China

detail.title: Educating like China
detail.abstract: This paper shows that human capital accumulation can accelerate structural transformation without accelerating growth. We study China's 1999 higher education expansion, a large, rapid, and largely unanticipated increase in college graduates. We find that more exposed prefectures experienced larger increases in the skilled-labor share and shifted employment and value added from agriculture toward services. The reallocation extended to low-skilled workers. Consumer services absorbed most of the increase in employment, while producer services accounted for a disproportionate share of high-skilled employment growth. Yet more-exposed prefectures did not grow faster. A four-sector model rationalizes these patterns, showing how greater skill supply can generate broad-based servitization, but also a Baumol-type growth penalty when labor reallocates toward slower-growing sectors. Our findings highlight that the payoff to higher education depends not only on how much skill it creates, but also on whether the resulting structural transformation directs resources toward the economy’s engines of productivity growth.
